title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
hook: Let an LLM write itself 'notes to self' — reusable strategies distilled from its own solution attempts — and its math and logic reasoning improves, with self-written notes as good as a teacher's.
key_points: The idea: distill an LLM's own solution traces into natural-language abstractions — strategies and cautionary reminders — stored in a retrievable library.
Two ways to use them: retrieve relevant abstractions at inference time, or fold them into training prompts for reinforcement learning.
Both modes improve performance on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks.
Self-extracted abstractions match those extracted by a stronger teacher model.
The framework transfers across datasets and models — evidence LLMs can leverage distilled experience much as humans do.
content_html: People get better at a task by distilling experience into reusable lessons — "try this strategy," "watch out for that trap" — and applying them next time. This paper asks whether LLMs can do the same with their own work.
extra_html:
A library the model writes for itself

Starting from an LLM's solution traces on the MATH training set, a stronger teacher (or the model itself) extracts natural-language abstractions — strategies and cautionary reminders — into a retrievable library. The authors then test two usage modes: retrieving relevant abstractions at inference time, and reinforcement learning with abstraction-augmented training prompts.

What it buys you

Both modes improve performance on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks, and self-extracted abstractions match teacher-extracted ones — the model doesn't need a smarter tutor to benefit. The framework also transfers to other datasets and models, suggesting that "learning from experience" through distilled, reusable notes is a general capability LLMs can exploit, not a one-off trick. Liu, Li, and Dubrawski, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
related.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.

related.title: ReAct: Reasoning + Acting
related.hook: Thinking alone can drift; acting alone is blind. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so an LLM can plan, look things up, and correct course — the template for agents.

related.title: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
related.hook: Self-improving agents are leaving the lab for production. This survey, co-authored by Jürgen Schmidhuber, gives the field a shared vocabulary for what an agent can update about itself, and what drives that update.

related.title: In-Context Learning
related.hook: Paste a few examples into a prompt and a large language model performs the task - no gradient updates, no fine-tuning, the prompt is the program.

flashcards.prompt: What are 'experiential abstractions' in this work?
flashcards.back_html: Reusable natural-language notes — strategies and cautionary reminders — distilled from an LLM's own solution traces and stored in a retrievable library for later reuse.

flashcards.prompt: How does self-extraction of abstractions compare to using a stronger teacher model?

choices.text: Self-extraction performs far worse than the teacher
Only teacher extraction gives any measurable benefit

flashcards.explanation_html: The model can distill useful abstractions from its own traces without a stronger teacher, and those self-extracted notes perform on par with teacher-extracted ones.

flashcards.prompt: What two ways did the authors use the abstraction library?
flashcards.back_html: Inference-time retrieval of relevant abstractions, and reinforcement learning with abstraction-augmented training prompts — both improved reasoning.
